title: The guard's hand
hookLine: Corrie ten Boom, who lost her sister in Ravensbrück, later took the hand of a former guard (The Hiding Place, 1971)

cards: A church in Munich, after the war. A Dutch woman named Corrie ten Boom has just finished speaking about forgiveness. One man comes forward instead, smiling, his hand held out, grateful for her message.
And she knows his face. In her memoir, The Hiding Place, she tells what came back: the camp called Ravensbrück, the uniform, the shame of the processing room, and her sister Betsie, who died there.
He doesn't seem to remember her. She remembers him. His hand is still out.

teach.b: First, who she was. In The Hiding Place, Corrie tells how her family, Christian watchmakers in the Dutch city of Haarlem, hid Jewish people in their house during the Nazi occupation.
They were betrayed and arrested, and she and Betsie were sent to Ravensbrück. Betsie, in Corrie's telling, kept talking about forgiveness even in the camp. She did not come home.
Second, the moment. In the church, the former guard thanks her for her message: his sins are washed away.
Corrie, who has just preached that very message, finds she can't lift her hand. She describes anger and a wish for revenge rising, knowing they were wrong, and being unable to make them go.
That honesty is the heart of the story: the one who taught forgiveness couldn't do it on her own.

teach.h: A PRAYER: I CANNOT, GIVE ME YOURS.
teach.b: Third, the prayer. In her account, she prays silently, telling Jesus she can't forgive him, and asks for the forgiveness she doesn't have. Then she takes his hand.

She describes something like a current between them, and a love she says was not her own. In her telling, forgiveness came as something given to her, not something she produced. Fourth, what it doesn't claim.
She doesn't say it was easy, or that the camp didn't matter, or that Betsie's death was fine. She tells it as a struggle she lost before help came.
Behind her stand Jesus's words in Matthew: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you." Her story doesn't make that command smaller.
It shows how heavy it is, and that one person, at least once, carried it across a church aisle.

how: Christians retell Corrie ten Boom's story, from her memoir The Hiding Place, when speaking about forgiving those who did terrible harm.

games.q: you're Corrie. a former guard from the camp where your sister died holds out his hand to shake yours. what does she do first?
o: stands frozen, unable to lift her hand.
games.why: she can't lift her hand. only after a silent prayer for help does she take it.

practice: This one asks for care: only if you're ready, let a very hard forgiveness come to mind, your own or one you've watched from close by.

You don't have to forgive anything today; just be honest the way Corrie was, notice what rises, anger, grief, numbness, and let it be there, then ask one small question: what would make this possible, even for a moment?
If you pray, you can ask, as she did, for help with what you can't do alone.

wordCard.voice: Ravensbrück. The camp where Corrie ten Boom's sister died, and where the guard whose hand she later took had served. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: hard, and possible. Nothing here has to be forced. That's day nine hundred fifty-four.
